A lot of people believe wealth is only for the “lucky” or the “already rich.”

But this chart shows something different — it shows that anyone can climb out of poverty if they’re consistent. You don’t need a PhD in finance. You don’t need a six-figure job. All you need is the discipline to invest small amounts over a long period of time.

And no — I’m not telling you to stop drinking coffee. Buy your latte. Enjoy your fried chicken. That’s not the point.

The point is this: after you buy that latte… put the same amount into your investments.
This isn’t replacing your budget — it’s supplementing it. Because the first person that needs to get paid in your household is YOU.

$5/day = $150/month → $206,000 in 30 years
Now imagine if instead of coffee money you invested your car note money.
$450/month → $618,000 in 30 years

That’s the difference between poverty and wealth.
That’s the kind of consistency that can close the racial wealth gap.

Be an investor first. Spend second.

My father was on blood pressure medication for 16 years. The cough that never stopped. The dizziness that made him fall twice. The exhaustion that turned him into a ghost of who he used to be. Last year, I saw the same numbers on my own monitor. I refused to follow his path.

And by the end of this, you're gonna be pissed.

Because there are three things happening right now:

One — Your blood pressure is creeping toward the same numbers your father had before they put him on medication

Two — The medical system has exactly one solution: pills for the rest of your life that manage the symptom but never fix the cause

Three — There's research from UCLA showing another approach, and nobody in that system will ever mention it to you

Let me tell you about my father. Because his story is why I spent six months researching blood pressure instead of just filling the prescription.

My father was on blood pressure medication for sixteen years.

It started when he was 54. Doctor said his BP was "getting into dangerous territory." 152/96. Wrote him a prescription for Lisinopril. Said it was "safe and effective." Said he'd probably be on it for life but that was "normal for someone his age."

Within three months, the cough started.

Not a normal cough. A dry, hacking, relentless cough that came out of nowhere. Middle of dinner. Middle of the night. Middle of a conversation. It never stopped.

My mother said it was like living with someone who was perpetually sick.

His doctor said it was "a common side effect" and "most patients adjust."

He didn't adjust. The cough continued for two years before they finally switched him to something else.

Amlodipine.

The cough stopped. But then his ankles started swelling.

Every single day. By evening, his ankles were so swollen he couldn't wear normal shoes. He'd sit in his recliner with his feet up, watching TV, wearing slippers because nothing else fit.

And the exhaustion.

My father used to coach my Little League team. He'd throw batting practice for an hour, then take us all for ice cream. Energy for days.

On the medication? He'd come home from work at 6 PM and be asleep by 7:30. Couldn't stay awake through a movie. Couldn't make it through dinner without yawning. My mother said it was like watching the man she married slowly disappear.

He fell twice.

Once in the garage — lost his balance, hit his head on the concrete floor. Eight stitches.

Once getting out of bed in the middle of the night. My mother found him on the bathroom floor at 3 AM, confused, not sure how he'd gotten there.

The doctors called it "orthostatic hypotension." Said it was "manageable." Added another medication to help with the dizziness.

So now he was on two blood pressure medications. Still exhausted. Still swollen ankles. Still falling.

And his blood pressure? "Controlled." Sitting at 134/86.

Not fixed. Controlled.

For sixteen years, my father took those pills every morning. For sixteen years, he dealt with side effects that made him miserable. For sixteen years, not one single doctor ever said: "Let's look at what's actually causing your blood pressure to be high instead of just medicating it forever."

He died at 70. Heart attack.

His blood pressure was "controlled" the entire time.

I was 51 when he died. And I made myself a promise standing at his grave.

I will not go down that path.

I will not spend the last decades of my life exhausted, dizzy, swollen, and "controlled."

I will find another way.

Three years later, I was sitting in my own doctor's office.

She wrapped the cuff around my arm. Pumped it up. Watched the numbers.

"147 over 94."

She frowned. Did it again.

"148 over 96."

She looked at me with that expression I recognized immediately. The same expression my father's doctor probably had twenty years ago.

"Your blood pressure is elevated. Stage 2 hypertension. We should talk about starting medication."

I felt my chest tighten.

"What medication?"

"Lisinopril is usually where we start. It's well-tolerated by most patients."

Lisinopril. The same drug that gave my father a two-year cough.

"Are there other options? Before medication?"

She nodded. "Lifestyle changes. Reduce sodium. Exercise more. Lose weight. We can try that for three months and see if your numbers improve."

I did everything she said.

Cut sodium to under 1,500mg a day. Walked 45 minutes every morning. Lost 11 pounds. Ate more vegetables than I'd eaten in my entire life combined.

Three months later: 143/91.

Four points.

She pulled out her prescription pad.

"I think it's time we start the Lisinopril."

I looked at that pad and I felt rage building in my chest.

Not at her. She was doing her job. Following her training.

At the system.

The system that put my father on medication for sixteen years and never once tried to fix the actual problem.

The system that was about to do the exact same thing to me.

"I want more time," I said.

She wasn't happy. Gave me a speech about "the risks of uncontrolled hypertension." Said we were "playing with fire."

A research paper from UCLA. A cardiologist named Dr. Matthew Budoff. Published in peer-reviewed journals.

Your endothelium is the inner lining of your blood vessels. It produces nitric oxide — the molecule that tells your arteries to relax and widen. When your endothelium is working properly, blood flows easily. Pressure stays normal.

BOTOX® Cosmetic (onabotulinumtoxinA) is a prescription medicine that is injected into muscles and used to temporarily improve the look of moderate to severe forehead lines, crow's feet, and frown lines between the eyebrows in adults.
-
Talk to your doctor about BOTOX® Cosmetic and whether it’s right for you. There are risks with this product—the effects of BOTOX® Cosmetic may spread hours to weeks after injection causing serious symptoms. Alert your doctor right away as difficulty swallowing, speaking, breathing, eye problems or muscle weakness can be a sign of a life-threatening condition. If this happens, do not drive a car, operate machinery, or do other dangerous activities. Patients with these conditions before injection are at the highest risk. Swallowing problems may last for several months. Side effects may include allergic reactions, neck and injection-site pain, fatigue and headache. Allergic reactions can include rash, welts, asthma symptoms, and dizziness. Don’t receive BOTOX® Cosmetic if there’s a skin infection. Tell your doctor your medical history, muscle or nerve conditions (including ALS/Lou Gehrig's disease, myasthenia gravis, or Lambert-Eaton syndrome), and medications, including botulinum toxins, as these may increase the risk of serious side effects.

BOTOX® Cosmetic (onabotulinumtoxinA) is a prescription medicine that is injected into muscles and used to temporarily improve the look of moderate to severe forehead lines, crow's feet, and frown lines between the eyebrows in adults. 
-
Talk to your doctor about BOTOX® Cosmetic and whether it’s right for you. There are risks with this product—the effects of BOTOX® Cosmetic may spread hours to weeks after injection causing serious symptoms. Alert your doctor right away as difficulty swallowing, speaking, breathing, eye problems or muscle weakness can be a sign of a life-threatening condition. If this happens, do not drive a car, operate machinery, or do other dangerous activities. Patients with these conditions before injection are at the highest risk. Swallowing problems may last for several months. Side effects may include allergic reactions, neck and injection-site pain, fatigue and headache. Don’t receive BOTOX® Cosmetic if there’s a skin infection. Tell your doctor your medical history, muscle or nerve conditions, and medications, including botulinum toxins, as these may increase the risk of serious side effects.

what you’ll need:
Breyers CarbSmart Vanilla 
2 eggs
1/2 cup Greek yogurt 
1/2 cup peanut butter (or other nut butter)
1/3 cup maple syrup
1 tsp vanilla extract
1/2 cup chocolate or unflavored protein powder
1/3 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
1/4 cup almond flour or oat flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/4 cup unsweetened dark chocolate chips (optional)

Instructions:
1. Preheat your oven to 350°F. Line an 8×8-inch baking pan with parchment paper and set aside.
2. In a large bowl, whisk together the eggs, Greek yogurt, nut butter, maple syrup, and vanilla until smooth and well combined.
3. Add the cocoa powder, protein powder, almond flour, baking powder, and salt. Stir until a thick, fully mixed batter forms.
4. If using, gently fold in the dark chocolate chips.
5. Pour the batter into the prepared pan and spread it evenly.
6. Bake for 18 to 22 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out with moist crumbs. Be careful not to overbake, these are best when fudgy.
7. Let the brownies cool completely in the pan before slicing into squares.
8. Top with a scoop of Breyers CarbSmart Vanilla and enjoy!

Why every menopausal woman should be grounding
"Are you seeing someone?" That's what my husband asked me last Tuesday. Dead serious.

I was so shocked. I just stared at him confused. 

"What? No. Why would you even…"

"Something’s up with you. You're different. You've been different for weeks. You're... happier all the sudden. So I thought maybe..."

I started crying. Not sad crying. Just... I didn't realize how bad things had gotten between us until he said that.

Let me back up.

I'm 52. For the past two years, menopause has been destroying me. And destroying my marriage.

The night sweats meant I was up at 2am every night, which meant he was up too. I'd have to change my pajamas, sometimes even put a towel down on the sheets. We were both exhausted.

The mood swings were worse. I'd snap at him over the tiniest things. He'd leave a cup on the counter and I'd lose it. Then I'd feel guilty and apologize, but the damage would already be done.

Slowly we started avoiding each other. Stopped talking. Stopped touching. We were just existing in the same house.

I'd tried everything. Expensive hormone creams. Supplements that did nothing. My doctor basically said "this is normal, you'll get over it."

I was adjusting to being miserable. And so was my husband.

Then about two months ago, I saw this article pop up on Facebook. It was written by a gynecologist from New York, and it was something about menopause not just being about hormones.

I almost scrolled past it. But I clicked.

She was talking about how there's this deeper issue that makes menopausal symptoms so much worse. 

She mentioned grounding therapy and how grounding sheets helped many of her patients.

(I don't remember all the exact details. If you want to read it, I've linked it below.)

It sounded absolutely insane. 

But at that point, I'd already wasted money on everything else. And this had a 90-day money-back guarantee.

I ordered the GroundingWell bedsheet without telling my husband. When it arrived, I opened the box in the bedroom.

He walked in and saw me laying out this long rectangular strip across our bed.

"What is that?"

"It's a grounding sheet. It goes on top our sheet and it—"

"How much did you spend?"

I told him.

He just closed his eyes and sighed. "Another thing that won't work. Great."

"They have a 90-day guarantee."

"We both know you're not going to actually return it."

I stayed silent.

“I’ll just put it on my side of the bed, then.”

I laid the sheet and plugged the cord into the outlet. My husband just shook his head and got into bed on his side, as far away from it as possible.

First night, I slept through without waking up drenched. I thought it was a fluke.

But it happened again the next night. And the night after that.

By the end of the first week, I realized I'd slept through the entire night seven days in a row. For the first time in 3 years, by the way.

I didn't say anything to my husband about it, but I started feeling… better? I had more energy. I wasn't as annoyed at everything.

About 10 days in, he said something at breakfast.

"You seem to be in a brighter mood nowadays," with a suspicious look on his face.

"Yeah."

He didn't say anything else. Just went back to his coffee.

Then I started noticing him doing strange things — things he hadn’t done in a while. He'd ask me about my day and actually listen to my answer. He'd make the bed in the morning, which he never did. Slowly but surely, we were talking again.

Three weeks in, I woke up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom. When I came back to bed, I noticed my husband had moved. He was sleeping diagonally, with half of his body on the grounding sheet.

I didn't think much of it. 

But it kept happening. Every few nights, I'd wake up and he'd be on my side of the bed.

Then one Saturday morning, I got up early to make coffee. When I came back upstairs, he was awake, sitting on the edge of the bed.

"I need to tell you something," he said.

"What is it?"

"I think there’s something to the sheets you got."

“What do you mean?” I said.

"To be honest my back has been killing me for a while. I didn’t want to tell you because you were dealing with enough. But I could barely sleep. And then I noticed when I accidentally rolled onto your side one night, I ended up sleeping through the night. Didn’t have the aches in the morning, either."

"So you've been sleeping on the grounding sheet." I said, with the I-told-you-so look.

"Yeah. And my back is better. Not completely gone, but better than it's been in months."

He looked at me. "I guess there’s something to it. I'm sorry I gave you a hard time about buying it. I wouldn’t mind you putting it across the bed."

That was six weeks ago.

Last week, we were at dinner with our friends. 

Our friend Kate, who’s also going through menopause, was talking about her experience—night sweats, exhaustion, mood swings. All of it.

My husband said, "You should try a grounding sheet."

I was shocked. Almost spit out my wine. This man who rolled his eyes when I bought it was now recommending it to our friends.

He pulled out his phone and sent the article I'd read. Sent it to her right then and there.

"GroundingWell is the company. They let you try it for 90 days. So give it a shot."

She ordered one right then and there. Then she texted me three days later: "I haven’t slept this good in years. I love the sheets, thank your husband for me!"

But the thing that got me was Tuesday night. When he asked if I was having an affair.

After I stopped crying, he said: "The past couple of years, it felt like you were here but never actually here. And then a few weeks ago, all the sudden you came back and seemed happier. I didn't know what changed, I just knew you were different, and just thought maybe…"

“No, of course not,” I said. 

"I'm actually sleeping properly for the first time in a long time. I have the energy to do things, and everything else feels better. That’s what’s changed."

"It's not just that. You're you again. We're us again."

He was right. We'd gone from barely speaking to actually talking every day. From sleeping on opposite sides of the bed to waking up next to each other. From existing together to actually being married again.

A bedsheet didn't save my marriage. But it gave me enough sleep and enough energy to show up as myself again. And that changed everything.

Here's what I learned about why GroundingWell actually works:

It's woven with pure silver fiber that conducts the earth's electrons while you sleep. The cord plugs into your outlet's ground port—the third hole that's literally connected to the earth outside.
Those electrons help reduce inflammation and balance cortisol, which is why it helps with night sweats and sleep.

I didn't set out to fix my marriage. I just wanted to sleep.

But I learned that when you finally sleep like you were supposed to and feel like yourself again, everything else just falls in line.

If you're going through menopause and you've noticed it's affecting more than just your sleep—your relationships, your patience, your ability to show up as yourself—read this article. 

It explains everything better than I can. It’s where I got the sheet, and it’s where everything started for me.

And if your husband is skeptical, just get it anyway. Give it a few weeks. Because even he might be surprised.

If someone depends on your income, you need term life insurance. Period.

I’ve said it for decades, and I’ll keep saying it: Life insurance isn’t about you. It’s about protecting the people you love.

If you died tomorrow, how would your family keep the lights on? Pay the mortgage? Afford groceries?

That’s where term life insurance steps in. It replaces your income so your family can stay afloat during the worst-case scenario. It’s not flashy, but it’s essential.

And this isn’t just for parents working outside of the house. If you’re a stay-at-home parent, you need life insurance too.

Think about everything you do in a day: child care, cleaning, cooking, transportation. If something happened to you, your spouse would need to pay for all those services—and that adds up fast. Term life coverage can make sure your family has the help they need to keep going.

Don’t fall for the whole life insurance scams. They cost more and cover less. And they’re stuffed with gimmicks that make insurance companies rich, not you.

Term life insurance is simple, affordable, and does exactly what you need it to do: cover your family while they still depend on you.

I recommend a 15- or 20-year term policy worth 10–12 times your annual income. That way, your family could invest the payout and live off the growth without touching the principal.

It takes less than five minutes to find out what it would cost you. Use this free tool to get your personalized estimate: https://ter.li/Term_Life_Estimate

Protect your family. Sleep better tonight.

A term policy lasts for a set number of years (usually 20) and you pay a low rate each month for the coverage you need. At the end of that term, yes, that policy has ended, but what the critics fail to remember is that you've had 20 years of affordable coverage. In that time, you can use the money you're saving to pay off debt, save for emergencies, and invest the difference you would have thrown away on a more expensive whole life policy.

If you're working to get out of debt and following the 7 Baby Steps, you'll be covered with your investments after 20 years, and you won't need life insurance anymore.

Don't throw your money away. Think for yourself and get the coverage you need, not the policy that someone making a commission wants to sell you on.

I recommend you get 10 to 12 times your annual income worth of term coverage.

For stay-at-home parents, I recommend a 15- to 20-year policy of at least $250,000–400,000.

I calculated what my clients actually spend on "affordable" towels. The number shocked me.
I've been designing luxury bathrooms for over a decade.
And there's one conversation I have with almost every new client.

It usually happens when we're picking out towels.
They'll point to something from a department store catalog and say, "These look fine. Why would I spend more?"

I used to nod and move on.

But a few years ago, I started keeping track.

Not of my opinion.

Of actual replacement cycles.

Here's what I found.

The average homeowner replaces their "affordable" towels every 12 to 18 months.

Sometimes sooner.

They start soft in the store.

But after a few washes, the fibers compress.

They shed little bits of lint all over your bathroom.
They scratch against your skin.
They stop absorbing water properly.

And eventually, they just look… tired.

So you throw them out and buy new ones.

And the cycle repeats.

I did the math for one client.

She was buying a $25 towel set from Target every year.

Over five years, that's $125 spent on towels that never felt right after the first month.

She thought she was being practical.

She was actually paying more for less.

This is the part most people don't realize.

Cheap towels aren't cheap.

They're expensive in disguise.

You pay less upfront.

But you pay more over time.

In replacements.
In frustration.
In never quite having that bathroom that feels finished.

I started recommending a different approach to my clients.

Stop buying towels like they're disposable.

Start buying towels like they're furniture.

Something you invest in once and enjoy for years.

That's when I discovered what hotels have known for decades.

The towels that actually last, the ones that feel like a spa experience every single day, are built differently.

They use 600 GSM Egyptian cotton.

That's the weight and density of the fabric.

Most retail towels sit around 300 to 400 GSM.

That's why they feel thin.

Because they are thin.

Hotel-quality towels also use something called zero-twist weave construction.

It creates soft, plush loops that stay fluffy wash after wash.

Traditional towels use a tighter twist.

It's cheaper to manufacture, but the fibers get rougher over time.

That's why your towels start soft and end up feeling like sandpaper.

I found a company called Onuia that builds towels the way hotels do.

600 GSM long-staple Egyptian cotton.

Zero-twist weave.

Reinforced edges that don't fray.

And here's what surprised me most.

They actually get softer with every wash.

Not rougher.
Softer.

Three years later, my clients tell me their Onuia towels still feel brand new.

Compare that to replacing department store towels every year.

A $25 towel that lasts 12 months costs you $125 over five years.

An Onuia towel at $36 that lasts five years costs you $36.

You're not just saving money.

You're buying out of the cheap product cycle entirely.

No more shedding.
No more scratching.
No more replacing towels that should have lasted longer.

Just thick, plush, absorbent towels that feel like a five-star hotel every single morning.

I now specify Onuia for every bathroom I design.

Not because they're the most expensive option.

Because they're the smartest one.

Right now, Onuia is offering up to 60% off with free shipping.

That means hotel-quality towels cost less than the thin, rough ones most people settle for.

Try them risk-free for 30 days.

If they're not the best towels you've ever owned, you get a full refund.

No questions asked.

Cheap towels cost more than you think.

The right towels cost less than you'd expect.

Phase 3 study design: ASCLEPIOS I and II were 2 identical, randomized, active-controlled, double-blind Phase 3 studies in patients with RMS, approximately 40% of whom were DMT treatment naïve. Patients were randomized to double-dummy SC KESIMPTA (20 mg every 4 weeks) or oral Aubagio® (teriflunomide) (14 mg daily) for up to 30 months. Primary end point was ARR. Key secondary end points were number of Gd+ T1 lesions and annualized rate of NE T2 lesions, and reduction in risk of 3-month CDP. Treatment duration was variable based on end-of-study criteria. Maximum duration: 120 weeks; median duration: 85 weeks.1

ARR, annualized relapse rate; CDP, confirmed disability progression; DMT, disease-modifying therapy; Gd+, gadolinium-enhancing; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; NE, new or enlarging; RMS, relapsing multiple sclerosis; SC, subcutaneous.

Please see full Prescribing Information, including Medication Guide, here: https://qr.qrhub.ly/KESIMPTA-PI

If you think that your high school counselor, financial advisor, or the college financial aid office would tell you if you were making expensive mistakes on your FAFSA, I’m sorry to say but you’re in for a rude and costly awakening.

That's exactly why I created a free training called "Cut your Student Aid Index for US families going to US Colleges & Universities."

It shows you why nobody in the system has any incentive to tell you what NOT to report, leaving families to accidentally sabotage their own aid eligibility.

Because when the people you trust for guidance stay silent about FAFSA exemptions, you end up paying tens of thousands more than necessary.

Here's what most families don't realize about the systemic silence around FAFSA mistakes and why nobody is coming to save you:

The first thing is, high school counselors don't know the financial details: Your counselor helps hundreds of students with college applications, test prep, and deadlines. They're not trained financial aid experts, and they're certainly not reviewing your specific asset reporting line by line.

They might tell you "fill out the FAFSA" but they're not going to catch that you reported $500,000 in retirement accounts that should be exempt.

The second thing - financial advisors focus on investments, not college aid: Your advisor knows portfolio management and retirement planning, but college financial aid calculations? That's a completely different specialty.

They won't review your FAFSA to catch over-reported assets because it's not their area of expertise. Meanwhile, their silence costs you $25,000+ per year.

The third thing - colleges benefit from your mistakes: Here's the uncomfortable truth: when you over-report assets on your FAFSA, you qualify for less aid, which means the college keeps more of your money.

Financial aid offices aren't going to proactively audit your FAFSA looking for exemptions you missed. They'll process what you submitted and move on. It's not their job to reduce your costs.

Let me tell you what this silence costs families: One family reported their $450,000 home equity on the FAFSA for two years straight.

Their high school counselor? Never mentioned it doesn't belong there.

Their financial advisor? Never reviewed their FAFSA.

The college financial aid office? Processed it without question.

Result? Over $50,000 in lost aid that nobody told them about until it was too late.

Here's why this systemic silence exists: It's not malicious - it's just that nobody in the traditional system has the specific expertise or incentive to optimize your FAFSA reporting.

Counselors are overwhelmed with applications. Advisors focus on investments. Colleges want tuition revenue.

You're on your own to figure out that retirement accounts, primary home equity, cars, life insurance cash value, and way more exemptions than 99% of parents realize shouldn't be on your FAFSA.

I'm putting on a free workshop that reveals all the exemptions nobody tells you about and shows you exactly what should and shouldn't be reported on your FAFSA.

The 'Weird Sheet' In Our 5-Star Airbnb
A guest just booked my Airbnb for the 8th time this year. She lives 20 minutes away. When I finally asked why, she broke down crying.

"I know this is going to sound insane, but I can't sleep at my own house anymore. I work night shifts as a nurse. The pain from standing 12 hours is destroying me. But here? I actually recover. So I come here once a month just to feel human again."

That's what Jennifer told me after I finally asked why she kept booking my Airbnb every single month.

She lives 20 minutes down the road.

She was spending $800 a month to sleep somewhere that wasn't her own bed.

And she was crying when she told me.

But let me back up.

So my husband and I have been running a five-star Airbnb for the past 4 years.

And about 7 months ago, I started noticing something strange.

A guest named Jennifer booked for a weekend. Called it a "staycation."

I thought it was a little odd since she mentioned living locally, but people do that sometimes. They want to get away without actually traveling.

She checked out and left a glowing review: "Slept better than I have in years."

Three weeks later, she booked again.

Then again a month after that.

By the fourth booking, I was genuinely confused.

Why would someone who lives 20 minutes away keep paying $200 a night to sleep somewhere else?

I finally asked her.

That's when she broke down.

"I'm a nurse," she said. "I work night shifts. Three 12-hour shifts a week. I'm on my feet the entire time."

Her voice cracked.

"My lower back is destroyed. My hips are shot. I go home after a shift and I can barely move. I take ibuprofen like candy just to function."

She paused, wiping her eyes.

"But when I stay here? I wake up and the pain is... manageable. I can think clearly. I have energy. I feel like myself again."

She'd been using my Airbnb as a monthly "reset" for her body.

One weekend a month where she could actually recover from the physical toll of her job.

"I know it sounds crazy to pay for this when I have a perfectly good bed at home," she said. "But I don't know what else to do. This is the only place I actually feel better."

That's when I told her about the grounding sheets.

She stared at me like I'd just told her the sky was green.

"The what?"

I explained everything. How they connect you to the Earth's electrical charge while you sleep. How the silver fibers conduct electrons that bring down inflammation.

She looked skeptical. But also desperate.

"If I buy these sheets for my own bed... will it be the same?"

I told her honestly: "I think so. But there's a 90-day guarantee if it doesn't work."

She ordered two sets that night. One for her bed. One for her mom who also works as a nurse and deals with chronic pain.

Two weeks later, I got this text:

"I haven't booked another stay. I don't need to anymore. I'm sleeping at home and waking up without pain for the first time in 3 years. I can't believe this is real."

That's when I realized how many people are living like Jennifer was.

Suffering every single day. Trying everything. And finding nothing that actually works.

But Jennifer's story isn't even the most heartbreaking one.

Last month, a guest named David checked in. He's a chef in his late 30s, works in a high-end restaurant downtown.

When he arrived, his hands were shaking.

Not from nerves. From pain.

"I have carpal tunnel so bad I can barely hold a knife anymore," he told me. "I'm supposed to get surgery in two months, but I'm terrified I won't be able to work the same way after."

He was staying for five nights while his apartment was being renovated.

First morning, he came downstairs and stared at his hands.

"I don't understand," he said. "I woke up and they didn't hurt. I thought maybe I just slept in a weird position."

Second morning? Same thing.

By the third morning, he could open and close his fists without wincing.

By the fifth morning, he was doing prep work in my kitchen just to test his hands.

Full range of motion. No pain. No shaking.

"What is happening?" he asked. "I haven't felt like this in two years."

I told him about the grounding sheets.

He didn't even hesitate. Ordered three of them before he checked out.

One for his bed. One for his sous chef who has the same problem. One for his dad who has arthritis.

Three weeks later, he sent me this message:

"I canceled the surgery. My hand mobility is back to 90%. My chef knife feels normal again. I can work a full shift without my hands cramping up. You saved my career."

So let me tell you what these sheets actually do, because I was skeptical at first too.

Most people don't realize this, but your body builds up a positive electrical charge throughout the day. You're surrounded by Wi-Fi, electronics, phones, screens—all of it creates what's called "dirty electricity."

Your body stores it. And that stored charge? It drives inflammation.

Which leads to pain.
Which leads to nerve damage.
Which leads to broken sleep where you wake up feeling worse than when you went to bed.

Grounding sheets REVERSE that.

The silver fibers woven into the fabric act like a conductor. You plug the cord into the grounding port in your wall—the third hole in the outlet that's connected to the Earth outside—and while you sleep, electrons flow from the ground into your body.

Those electrons neutralize the inflammation. Your nervous system calms down. Your cortisol drops. Your body finally gets into deep, restorative sleep.

And when you wake up? Your back doesn't scream. Your hands don't shake. Your hips don't lock up.

You just feel... normal.

I bought my first GroundingWell sheet three years ago because I kept hearing about grounding from a friend who wouldn't stop talking about it.

I didn't think it would work. I thought it was complete nonsense.

But the first morning I woke up after using it, I sat up in bed and literally looked around confused.

My shoulders that had been chronically tight for years felt loose.

My husband noticed immediately. "You didn't toss and turn at all last night. Not once."

Within two weeks, the neck pain I'd had since my 30s was completely gone.

I wasn't expecting that. I just wanted better sleep.

That's when I bought sheets for the Airbnb. All four beds. And then our guest room at home. And then my mom's house because she wouldn't stop complaining about her arthritis.

We probably own seven or eight of these sheets now.

And the guest reviews? They transformed completely.

Before the grounding sheets, we'd get: "Great location, clean, comfortable."

After? "I've never slept better in my life. I need to know what sheets these are."

We've had guests rebook specifically to sleep in our beds again. We've had people offer to buy the sheets directly off us. One woman with fibromyalgia extended her stay by five nights because her pain dropped so dramatically she told me: "I'm scared to go home. I don't want it to come back."

That's not the mattress. That's not the pillows. That's not our thread count.

That's the grounding sheets.

Here's what I wish someone had told me three years ago:

Not all grounding sheets work. MOST of them are complete garbage.

We've tried 5 other brands, but GroundingWell is the only one we keep coming back to. Their sheets use pure silver fiber woven throughout the entire fabric—not just a coating that washes off after three uses like the cheap Amazon knockoffs.

The silver maintains conductivity. The organic cotton is breathable and soft. And the cord actually works—it's not some flimsy wire that stops conducting after a month.

That's why GroundingWell is the only one I trust. It's the only one I put in my Airbnb, because I can't risk guests having a bad experience.

And right now, they're running a sale. I just checked their site this morning and grabbed two more, one for my sister who's a teacher and deals with chronic back pain from standing all day, and one backup for the rental.

(To be honest, I panicked a little when I saw the sale because they sell out constantly. Last time they restocked, it took three months.)

If you're dealing with chronic pain, inflammation, carpal tunnel, nerve damage, or you work a physical job that's destroying your body, just try it.

We get a lot of questions from people who want to know what attending a midlife workshop at MEA is “really like.”

They’ve heard the buzz – but they’re skeptical.  

Even though they’ve read that our curriculum is based on social science – and was developed in collaboration with leading academics from Stanford, Harvard, UC Berkeley, and Yale – they’re still uncertain.  

Is there too much “woo” involved?  

Will it actually help them deal with the real and pressing challenges they’ve been experiencing in midlife?  

We get it – if you’ve never been, it can be hard to wrap your head around.  

Which is why we were so thrilled to see this article that award-winning writer Tom Ford wrote for Texas Monthly magazine about his experience attending an MEA workshop in Santa Fe earlier this summer.

Tom admits that he was skeptical about anything related to “self-help” and came to MEA partly because he wanted to challenge his prejudice.  

(AND because he legitimately wanted some guidance about some midlife challenges he was dealing with.) 

You can read the article he wrote about his experience here. 

If you’ve been wondering about what it’s like to attend an MEA workshop in person, we strongly encourage you to check it out! 

Especially if you’re a skeptic or wary of “woo.” 

Tom does an incredible job of bringing his experience to life and encapsulating the magic and authenticity of the MEA experience. 

 (And what he says about our “resident yoga cowboy weirdo” Lee Johnson and his socks had our entire team in stitches for a week.)

Airport security stopped me because of what I was wearing.

Best stop I've ever had.

Flying out of Dallas-Fort Worth. Coming back from a military funeral.

I'm wearing my DearPersonCo hoodie under my uniform because airports are freezing.

Going through TSA. Agent asks me to step aside.

I'm thinking I'm in trouble.

He goes, "I saw your hoodie when you put your jacket in the bin. What's it say?"

I show him.

"You are enough."

And on the back: "Dear person behind me, the world is better with you in it."

He gets quiet.

Then tells me his son's a Marine. Just got back from deployment. Won't talk to anyone.

He asks where to buy the hoodie.

Says maybe his son will wear it. Maybe it'll help.

I told him about DearPersonCo.
How it was started by someone who lost her sister to su!cide.
And that a portion of every sale goes to mental health nonprofits. 
He bought 2 hoodies right there, one for him, one for his son. 
Then he does something I'll never forget. 

Salutes me.

Not for my service. For the hoodie.

Says "Thank you for wearing that. More of us need to."

That wasn't the first time.

Three weeks later. Layover in Atlanta.

Woman behind me at Starbucks taps my shoulder.

She's tearing up before she even says anything.

Tells me her brother took his life last year. She's been wearing all black ever since.

She took a picture of the back of my hoodie and sent it to her mom right there.

Two days after that. Gate B7 in Chicago.

Pilot walks up to me. Full uniform.

He doesn't say much. Just points at my hoodie and goes, "I needed to see that today. Thank you."
But it didn't stop there.

Different airports. Different people. Same reaction.

They make these specifically for moments like that.

I travel a lot for work now. Wear this hoodie every single time.

Since that TSA stop, I've had four more agents, two flight attendants, and a pilot stop me about it.

And every time, I think the same thing.

You never know what they're carrying.
You never know who's standing behind you.

Your back might be the only thing they see today that says "Stay."

Get yours at DearPersonCo before they sell out again.

Wear it. Be the reason someone keeps going.

Kaspi.kz (Nasdaq: KSPI) today announced that Tencent, Kaspi.kz Co-Founder and CEO Mikheil Lomtadze, key members of the senior management team, and long-term institutional investors have completed the purchase of 6.0 million American Depositary Shares (ADSs) from Baring Fintech Venture Funds (the “Funds”).

Mikheil Lomtadze, CEO and Co-Founder of Kaspi.kz, commented:

“Tencent pioneered the super app ecosystem business model, and we have long admired its ability to combine innovation at scale with disciplined execution. We are delighted to welcome Tencent as one of Kaspi.kz’s largest shareholders.

My own investment, together with those of key members of our senior management team, reflects our strong belief in Kaspi.kz’s Super App business model, long-term strategy and future growth opportunities.

We are also pleased to welcome Spice Expeditions, a globally focused fintech investment firm, and the U.S. university endowments of Washington University and WISIMCO / University of Wisconsin Foundation, as long-term shareholders. 

The combination of strategic, management and highly respected institutional capital comes at an exciting time for Kaspi.kz as we build on our market leadership in Kazakhstan and expand into Türkiye.”
Morgan Stanley acted as exclusive financial advisor to the Funds on the transaction.

About Kaspi.kz

Kaspi.kz’s mission is to improve people’s lives by developing innovative mobile products and services. 

Kaspi.kz operates a unique two-sided Super App model, serving more than 25 million consumers and 900 thousand merchants across Kazakhstan and Türkiye. In Kazakhstan, our Super App seamlessly integrates payments, e-commerce, e-grocery, fintech, travel, classifieds and government services. This comprehensive offering is deeply relevant to users’ daily lives, driving exceptional engagement with 77 monthly transactions per active consumer. In Türkiye, Kaspi.kz owns an 86% stake in Hepsiburada, one of the country’s leading e-commerce platforms. 

Kaspi.kz has been listed on Nasdaq since January 2024.

A high school project humbled me today
My 16-year-old just texted me a screenshot and I don't know whether to be proud or humiliated.

She got her learner's permit three weeks ago. Hasn't driven on a real road yet. Still parks like she's defusing a bomb.

But for some school project on "adulting," her teacher had them pull a quote on what it would cost to insure their own hypothetical car. A used 2018 Civic. Just to see.

She sent me the number. $89 a month.

I'm 43. Clean record. Drive a 2019 Accord. I pay $237.

I asked her how she got that number. She said the teacher gave them a site to use — some quiz thing. Took her like two minutes during 4th period.

So I sat in my driveway after work and did the same thing. Same site she used. Honest answers. My car, my zip, my actual record.

$47 a month.

I've been with the same company since I bought my first truck in 2007. Eighteen years of on-time payments, no accidents, no tickets. And a kid who's never legally driven a car just out-shopped me in a high school classroom on her lunch break.

She asked me at dinner if I was going to switch. I told her I already did it on my phone before she got home.

She just looked at me and goes, "Dad. I'm 16. You're supposed to be teaching me this stuff."

Fair.

The site her teacher gave them is below if you want to feel the same way I felt sitting in that driveway.

Your Body Responds to Physics, Not Motivation

If motivation worked, everyone with a gym membership would feel great.

But your body isn’t persuaded by willpower, discipline, or mindset.

It responds to physics.

It adapts to force, pressure, vibration, load, and flow.

That’s not a metaphor.

It’s how cells work.

Muscle activates when it receives mechanical signal.

Blood vessels adapt when they feel shear stress from circulation.

Bones strengthen under load.

Connective tissue remodels only when it’s mechanically stimulated in ways it can actually recognize.

Motivation can make you try.

It cannot make your joints tolerate repetitive strain.

It cannot speed up recovery when the system is under-signaled and over-stressed.

And that’s why people get stuck.

They push harder, “stay consistent,” and end up tight, inflamed, sore, and frustrated… even when they’re doing everything right.

Especially after 35 or 40.

Because the issue isn’t character.

It’s input quality.

This is where Power Plate is different, because it delivers the mechanical signal directly, without asking your joints to absorb impact and without requiring you to “work yourself into” activation.

You don’t have to run.

You don’t have to lift.

You don’t have to be flexible.

You don’t have to be in shape to start.

You step on.

You stand.

The platform does the work of delivering high-frequency mechanical input that your body can feel instantly—through muscles, circulation, and neuromuscular activation—without the wear-and-tear of traditional workouts.

This is why “standing on it” is not a gimmick.

It’s the point.

It’s the simplest way to give the body the kind of physical signal it recognizes as movement, without needing motivation to carry the load.

Nine minutes of standing can be enough to change how your body feels that day.

Not because it’s magic.

Because physics is reliable.

And because when the signal is right, the body responds.

Power Plate turns activation into something anyone can do, regardless of age, fitness level, injury history, or schedule, because it doesn’t require intensity; it requires consistency, and consistency is easy when the barrier is basically zero.

If you can stand, you can activate.

And once you feel what activation does—less stiffness, better movement, quicker recovery—you stop thinking of it as “exercise.”

You start thinking of it as the missing daily input your biology has been waiting for.

My CO Detector Almost Killed My Family
I've been a firefighter for 7 years. Nine months ago, I went home at 4 AM and ripped every detector off my own walls.

I thought I'd seen everything.

House fires. Car accidents. Medical emergencies. All of it.

But nothing prepared me for the call we got at 1:47 AM on a Tuesday in May.

"Family of four. Possible carbon monoxide. Ambulance en route."

We pulled up to a quiet suburban street. Lights on in the house. Front door wide open.

A man was standing on the lawn in his pajamas. Two kids sitting on the grass wrapped in blankets. A woman on her knees throwing up.

Neighbor was with them. She's the one who called 911.

"I couldn't sleep," she said. "Saw them stumble outside. Something's very wrong."

I grabbed my meter and went inside.

The reading hit me before I even made it to the hallway.

48 PPM in the living room. 67 PPM near the bedrooms. Over 90 PPM in the basement.

This family had been breathing poison all night.

I walked back outside.

The paramedics were putting oxygen masks on the kids. The mom was still dry heaving. The dad looked pale, disoriented.

"How long were you inside?" I asked him.

"We went to bed around 10," he said. His words were slurred. "Woke up maybe 20 minutes ago. Something felt wrong."

"You got lucky," I said. "Another hour and we'd be having a very different conversation."

I went back inside to find the source.

Furnace in the basement. Heat exchanger had a crack you could barely see. Every time it fired up, carbon monoxide leaked into the ductwork and spread through the whole house.

Classic case.

But here's what got me.

As I was walking through the hallway, I saw it.

A carbon monoxide detector. Plugged into the wall outlet.

Little green light glowing.

I checked my meter again. 67 PPM right where I was standing.

The detector was silent.

I pulled it off the wall and brought it outside.

The dad saw me holding it.

"That's supposed to keep us safe," he said. "Why didn't it go off?"

I turned it over and checked the back.

First Alert. Manufactured in 2024.

"When did you buy this?" I asked.

"Six months ago," he said. "Right after we moved in. Got it at Lowe's."

"You test it?"

"Every month. It always beeps. The green light's always on."

His wife looked at me.

"I thought these things lasted seven years?"

"They do," I said. "But that's not the problem."

I showed them the reading on my meter.

"This detector is brand new. It's working perfectly. The sensor is fine. The battery is fine. The speaker works."

"Then why didn't it go off?" the dad asked.

"Because it's designed to wait until you hit 70 parts per million before it alarms."

They stared at me.

"Your levels were at 67. Right below the threshold. It was doing exactly what it's supposed to do."

"But we were dying," the mom said.

"I know."

I looked at the two kids wrapped in blankets. The boy couldn't have been more than eight. The girl looked about five.

"At 70 PPM, you've already been breathing poison for hours. You're already symptomatic. Headache. Nausea. Confusion. Your kids have been sleeping in it all night."

I paused.

"And that's if it's rising slow. If you've got a serious leak and levels jump fast, by the time this thing decides to beep, there's a very good chance you're already too sick, too confused, too weak to respond."

The dad just stared at the detector in my hand.

"But we did everything right," he said. "We bought a detector. We tested it. We thought we were safe."

"You're not the first family to think that," I said. "And you won't be the last."

The ambulance took them to the hospital. Oxygen therapy. Observation. They got lucky.

I went home that night around 4 AM.

My wife was asleep. My two daughters were in their rooms.

I walked into the hallway and looked at our detector.

Same brand. Same model. Same little green light glowing.

I'd tested it two weeks ago. It beeped loud. Green light came back on.

I thought that meant it worked.

I grabbed my work meter from my truck and walked through the house.

0 PPM everywhere. We were fine.

But I realized something that made my stomach turn.

If we ever DID have a leak, this detector wouldn't warn us until it was almost too late.

Just like that family.

I sat down at my kitchen table and started researching.

Those cheap detectors — the ones at Home Depot, Lowe's, Walmart, the ones in 90% of American homes — they're designed to meet minimum UL safety standards.

Not to actually save your life.

The UL standard requires them to alarm at 70 PPM within 60 to 240 minutes.

70 PPM. And they can take up to FOUR HOURS to make a sound.

And they're ALLOWED to stay completely silent at lower levels. 30 PPM? 40 PPM? 50 PPM? Levels that are absolutely dangerous, especially for kids and elderly people?

The detector doesn't have to do anything.

It's not broken. It's not defective. It's working exactly as designed.

And that design is killing people.

I went back to the station the next day and told the other guys.

One of the veterans, Martinez, pulled me aside.

"You remember that call three months ago? The family on Maple Street?"

I nodded. I'd been there.

Mom, dad, three kids. We found them in the morning. Neighbor called it in when the kids didn't show up for the school bus.

All five of them gone.

CO poisoning from a cracked heat exchanger.

"They had detectors," Martinez said. "Brand new. The levels built slowly all night. By the time they hit 70 PPM, the family was already too far gone. Too asleep. Too poisoned."

He paused.

"After that call, I was losing my mind. My brother-in-law's an HVAC tech. Been doing it for 20 years. I called him and asked what he uses in his own house."

He showed me his phone.

"Steadfast Haven. Said it's what all the HVAC guys use because they see furnace failures every single day. They know what the cheap ones miss."

It wasn't just a detector with a light. It had a digital display. Real-time PPM readings for both CO and natural gas.

"Alarms at 10 PPM," Martinez said. "Dual sensors. My brother-in-law said he wouldn't let his family sleep in a house without one."

That night, I ordered a 4-pack.

One for each floor. One near the furnace. One in the kitchen by the gas stove.

I pulled every old detector off the walls. Threw them in the trash.

Plugged in the new ones and watched the displays light up.

0 PPM CO. 0 PPM gas. Temperature reading. Humidity.

Real information. Not just a meaningless green light.

For the first time in my career, I actually felt like my family was protected.

Not because I hoped it would work.

Because I could see proof.

That was nine months ago.

And I haven't shut up about it since.

Every CO call I respond to, I tell them about Steadfast Haven. I show them the one I use. I explain why their detector failed them.

My wife thinks I'm obsessed. She's right.

Because I can't unsee what I've seen.

About five months ago, in September, dispatch sends us to a house three streets over from mine.

"CO alarm going off. Family evacuated. Requesting response."

It's the Hendersons. I'd responded to their house back in March for a small kitchen fire. When I left that day, I told them about their CO detector. They ordered a 4-pack that same week.

The whole family is standing on the lawn. Dad, mom, two teenage daughters. Shaken but fine.

"The detector started going off," Mr. Henderson says. "Woke us all up. We got out and called 911."

I go inside with my meter. 32 PPM in the hallway. 41 PPM in the bedrooms. 68 PPM in the basement near the furnace.

Their Steadfast Haven display showing 32 PPM CO. Alarm still going.

"Your furnace has a leak," I tell them. "Levels were at 10 PPM when the alarm first went off. By now they're over 40 and climbing."

Mr. Henderson looks at me.

"Our old detector's still in the garage. The one you told us to replace."

I take it inside and plug it in right next to the Steadfast Haven.

The Haven is still alarming. Display showing 43 PPM.

The old detector? Green light glowing. Silent.

I bring it back outside and show them.

"If you still had this one, you'd all be asleep right now. Breathing poison. In another few hours, we'd be having a very different conversation."

Mrs. Henderson started crying.

"You saved our lives," she said.

"No," I said. "That detector did."

HVAC company came out that morning. Cracked heat exchanger. Same as always.

But this family got out at 10 PPM. Wide awake. Alert. Safe.

Not at 70 PPM when they're already too sick to move.

That's the difference.

I think about that call in May all the time.

About that dad standing on his lawn asking me why his detector didn't work.

About his kids wrapped in blankets breathing oxygen.

They did everything right. Bought a detector. Tested it monthly. Saw the green light.

It was brand new. It wasn't expired. It wasn't broken.

It just wasn't designed to save them.

I've stood in driveways and told parents their kids didn't make it.

I've carried bodies out of houses that had working detectors on the walls.

I replaced every detector in my house, my parents' house, everywhere my family sleeps.

My wife checks them every morning. Four screens. Four zeros.

That's what safe actually looks like.

Not a green light that might mean something or might mean nothing.

Real data. Real protection.
